property_summary: For every oracle and payoffDefinition pair, C.currentVersion() must return the oracle's currentVersion with its price transformed by payoffDefinition().transform(...) (i.e. price != raw oracle price when transform changes it); the mutant returns the raw oracle price so there exist oracle/prices where the returned price differs and the property is violated.

For every oracle and payoffDefinition, C.currentVersion() returns the oracle's currentVersion with its price transformed by the product's payoffDefinition (i.e. returned.price == payoffDefinition.transform(raw.price)); the mutant returns the raw oracle price so there exist oracle prices where returned.price != transformed price.

For any deployed product C and any oracle that returns a currentVersion with price p, C.currentVersion() always returns that oracle version but with price transformed by the product's payoffDefinition (i.e. returned.price == payoffDefinition.transform(oraclePrice)); the mutant returns the raw oracle price for some oracle prices, so the equality can be broken.

For any oracle price, C.currentVersion() returns the oracle's currentVersion but with its price transformed by the product's payoffDefinition (i.e. returned.price == payoffDefinition().transform(oraclePrice)); the mutant returns the raw oracle price for some oracle prices, so there exist inputs where returned.price != transformed price.

For any oracle that reports a currentVersion, C.currentVersion() always returns that oracle version but with its price transformed by the product's payoffDefinition; the mutant returns the raw oracle price (no transform) and thus can produce a different price for some oracle outputs.

For any oracleVersion id, the reference contract's atVersion(...) returns the oracle's version with its price transformed by the product's payoffDefinition, whereas the mutant returns the raw oracle price (no transform) — so the transformed price must equal oracle().atVersion(id).price transformed via payoffDefinition, and the mutant will differ for inputs where transform changes the price.

For any oracleVersion id, C.atVersion(id) returns an OracleVersion whose price equals payoffDefinition().transform( oracle().atVersion(id).price ); the mutant omits the transform and thus for some ids (where transform changes price) the returned price will differ.

For every oracleVersion id, C.atVersion(id) returns an OracleVersion whose price equals payoffDefinition().transform( oracle().atVersion(id).price ); the mutant omits this transform so for some oracleVersion ids the returned price differs.

For every oracleVersion id, the correct contract's atVersion(id) returns an OracleVersion whose .price equals payoffDefinition().transform( oracle().atVersion(id).price ); the mutant returns the raw oracle price so there exists some oracleVersion id where the returned price differs.

For every oracleVersion id, C.atVersion(id) returns an OracleVersion whose price equals payoffDefinition().transform( oracle().atVersion(id).price ); the mutant omits the transform so there exists some oracleVersion id where the returned price differs.
For any product instance, maintenance() returns the stored _maintenance value; the mutant returns constant ONE instead, so for some stored _maintenance values (e.g. zero) the returned value differs.

For every stored maintenance parameter value X, the deployed reference contract returns maintenance() == X for any account; the mutant always returns ONE, so when the stored maintenance X != ONE the mutant's return differs and the property is violated.

For any stored maintenance parameter value set at initialize, calling maintenance(account) always returns that stored maintenance; the mutant that returns constant ONE will disagree whenever the stored maintenance differs from ONE (e.g., when initialized with ZERO), so the property is violated for those inputs.

For any ProductInfo.utilizationCurve and maintenance parameter given to initialize, the reference contract returns maintenance(account) equal to the stored maintenance value; the mutant always returns ONE, so when the stored maintenance differs from ONE the mutant's maintenance(account) return differs and the property is violated.

For any account and any stored maintenance parameter, the reference contract returns the stored maintenance value from maintenance(account); the mutant that hardcodes ONE will differ whenever the stored maintenance is not ONE, so there exist inputs where maintenance(account) differs between reference and mutant.

For every input the correct contract returns takerFee() equal to the stored _takerFee (i.e., not always zero); the mutant returns ZERO for all inputs, so there exist inputs where takerFee() != stored value causing the observable getter to differ.

For any stored non-zero taker fee value, the reference contract returns that stored value from takerFee(), whereas the mutant returns ZERO; thus the general rule: takerFee() equals the stored _takerFee (and can be non-zero) — the mutant breaks this by always returning ZERO.
